title: Angle of Light
question: What happens to the light reading as a light sensor is tilted away from facing the light?
curriculum: Energy can be transferred and transformed; light spreads over a larger area when it strikes a surface at an angle. Plan and conduct a fair investigation, process data, and communicate findings with evidence.
equipment: Desk lamp, light sensor or databot (optional), protractor
safety: The lamp gets hot. Don't look directly into the bulb.

plan.title: Angle of Light
plan.drivingQuestion: What happens to the light reading as a light sensor is tilted away from facing the light?
objectives: Measure light intensity in lux at three sensor angles
Describe the pattern: tilting spreads the same light over more area, so readings fall
Compare measured results with the cosine rule
Explain how the angle of sunlight causes the seasons
curriculumLinks: Energy transfer and transformation, including light

model.description: Light on a tilted surface falls with the cosine of the tilt angle, because the same beam spreads over more area.

interactives: Drag the databot to tilt it from 0° to 90°; photons, glow and beam-caught gauge respond live
Sensor tilt and light strength sliders
Autoplay at 1×, 2× or 4× moves through flat, halfway and almost sideways
Graph scrubber to read any point
noticeWonder: What do you notice about the reading while the databot lies flat?
What happened to the reading when it tilted halfway?
Almost sideways now: what do you notice, and what do you wonder?
plan.challenge: Find the tilt angle that halves the light reading (the answer is 60°, not 45°).
misconceptions: The Sun is closer to Earth in summer
Tilting changes how much light the lamp gives out
Half the tilt (45°) gives half the light
safety: The lamp gets hot. Don't look directly into the bulb.
stages: Drag the databot under the lamp and watch how much of the beam it catches
Pick a graph shape and explain why
Use the simulation, or a real lamp and light sensor
Record for 60 s while tilting to 45° and 75°, or press Autoplay; answer notice-and-wonder checkpoints; fill in the findings table
Read the graph, compare with the cosine rule, solve the half-light challenge
Nine CER questions with evidence hints from your own data

title: Pendulum Swing
question: How does the length of a pendulum change how long one swing takes?
curriculum: Investigate the motion of objects and the forces acting on them; use models and mathematical relationships to explain observed motion.
equipment: String, washers, retort stand, ruler, stopwatch
safety: Keep swinging bobs away from faces. Clamp the stand to the bench.

plan.title: Pendulum Swing
plan.drivingQuestion: Why does a grandfather clock need such a long pendulum?
objectives: Measure the period of a pendulum at five string lengths
Identify that length, not mass, controls the period
Recognise a square-root relationship from a curved graph
Explain why timing 10 swings reduces error

model.description: The period depends on the square root of the length: four times the length gives twice the period.

interactives: Drag the bob to change the string length; motion trail and period HUD update live
String length and bob mass sliders
Autoplay times every length at 1×, 2× or 4×
noticeWonder: You timed the shortest pendulum. What do you notice about how fast it swings?
How has the period changed as the string got longer?
Did doubling the length double the period?
misconceptions: Doubling the length doubles the period
safety: Keep swinging bobs away from faces. Clamp the stand to the bench.
stages: Drag the bob and change the mass; watch the period
Pick a graph shape and explain why
Simulation, or a real stand, string and stopwatch
Run trials at five lengths or press Autoplay; notice-and-wonder checkpoints; findings table
Graph, model overlay, one-second pendulum challenge

title: Dissolving Race
question: Does sugar dissolve faster in hotter water?
curriculum: Use the particle model to explain the properties of substances and the processes of dissolving.
equipment: Beakers, sugar cubes, kettle, thermometer, stopwatch
safety: Hot water scalds. Teacher pours water above 50 °C. Wear safety glasses.

plan.title: Dissolving Race
plan.drivingQuestion: Why does sugar vanish faster in hot tea than in iced tea?
objectives: Measure dissolving time at five water temperatures
Describe the pattern as a curve that levels off
Explain the pattern with the particle model
Identify variables to control for a fair test

model.description: Hotter water particles move faster and break the sugar apart sooner.

interactives: Drag up or down to heat the water; particles speed up and steam appears
noticeWonder: Cold water first. What do you notice about the particles and the time?
Now the water is warm. What's different?
Hottest water. What pattern do you see?
plan.challenge: Make the cube dissolve in one minute.
misconceptions: Sugar disappears, so it is gone
Hot water always halves the time
safety: Hot water scalds. Teacher pours water above 50 °C. Wear safety glasses.
stages: Heat the water and stir; watch the particles
Pick a graph shape and explain why
Simulation, or real beakers and a thermometer
Race five temperatures or press Autoplay; checkpoints; findings table

title: Light and Plant Growth
question: Do plants grow taller with more hours of light each day?
ivariable: Hours of light each day (0 to 16)
curriculum: Living things depend on each other and the environment; plants need light, water and air to grow.
equipment: Bean seeds, pots, potting mix, lamp, ruler
safety: Wash your hands after touching soil. Don't touch the hot lamp.

plan.title: Light and Plant Growth
plan.drivingQuestion: Do plants need light to grow tall?
objectives: Grow plants with different hours of light
Describe the pattern: more light, taller, up to a limit
Explain that plants use light to make food

model.description: Plants use light to make food, so more light means more growth, until something else runs short.

interactives: Drag the lamp to change the hours of light; day and night cycle in the time-lapse
Autoplay grows every plant over 21 days
noticeWonder: This plant had no light. What do you notice?
8 hours of light. How is it different?
16 hours of light. What do you wonder?
misconceptions: Plants get their food from the soil
More light always means more growth
safety: Wash your hands after touching soil. Don't touch the hot lamp.
stages: Move the lamp and change the water; watch the plant
Pick a graph shape and say why
Simulation, or real bean plants for 3 weeks
Grow five plants in time-lapse or press Autoplay; checkpoints; findings table
